## PART 1 — TITLE

Sent and Rejected: Trusting God's Word

---

## PART 2 — SCRIPTURE

Reading I: Yer 26:1-9

Gospel: Matius 13:54-58

---

## PART 3 — THEME

God's chosen messengers are often met with resistance from the very people who ought to recognize His voice. In Jeremiah, the prophet is threatened with death for speaking God's word in the temple, yet God's truth cannot be silenced. In Matthew, Jesus is rejected in His own hometown, where familiarity bred contempt. Both readings reveal a profound spiritual reality: the one who comes in God's name will be met with suspicion, but the Word of the Lord endures forever.

---

## PART 4 — HISTORICAL BACKGROUND

In Jeremiah 26, Jeremiah speaks God's word during the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah (around 609 BC). The prophet delivers a direct message in the Temple of the LORD in Jerusalem, warning that if the people do not repent and turn from their wicked ways, this temple will share the fate of Shiloh. By this period, Jerusalem had become a center of religious ritual, yet spiritual complacency and political anxiety about Babylon threatened to overwhelm the call to genuine conversion. Jeremiah speaks in the temple courts, a place of daily prayer and sacrifice, where his words challenge the religious establishment. The officials and elders convene at the New Gate of the temple to hear the case against him. They recall the precedent of Micah of Moresheth, who prophesied during the reign of King Hezekiah (around 700 BC) that Zion would be plowed as a field — yet Micah was honored by the community, not executed. This reminder of mercy toward faithful prophets highlights the danger of rejecting God's messengers.

In Matthew 13, Jesus returns to Nazareth, a modest village in Lower Galilee where He grew up among a close-knit agricultural community. The Greek term *tekton* — used here for Joseph's trade — refers to a builder or craftsman who worked with wood and stone. In first-century Jewish villages, such a laborer would be known by face, by craft, and by family. The people of Nazareth knew Mary, the brothers named James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas, and the sisters they grew up with. For them, holiness did not look like this. Jesus' teaching "astounded them," yet astonishment without faith produces only offense.

---

## PART 5 — SCRIPTURE MEDITATION

The temple courts of Jerusalem hummed with the ordinary rhythm of worship. Incense rose. Feet shuffled across stone. Voices murmured prayers the way voices do in places where religion has become comfortable. Then a voice cut through the noise — not raised in anger, but steady with the weight of God himself.

Jeremiah stood and spoke. He spoke what the LORD had given him to speak. He warned the people. He called them back. He spoke of a temple that could become a ruin if hearts remained far from God.

And the room erupted.

Priests seized him. Prophets shouted for his blood. The crowd closed in with the certainty that they knew better than the prophet standing before them. They had come to worship — and they had come to silence the voice of God.

But then the officials of Judah arrived. And the elders remembered Micah. A man who had spoken the same dangerous truth centuries earlier — and who had been honored, not destroyed, because his words came from the LORD.

God's Word does not depend on our approval. It does not wait for us to be ready. It does not pause when we resist it. It simply speaks — and asks only that we listen.

Centuries later, in a small village in Galilee, the same dynamic played out in a quieter, quieter room. The synagogue of Nazareth sat nestled among familiar hills, the very landscape where a boy named Jesus had learned to shape wood with His father's hands. When He stood to read and speak, the neighbors expected nothing extraordinary. They expected the carpenter's son. They expected nothing at all.

And yet what came from His lips was not the teaching of a local craftsman. It was something far greater. The people sensed this — and it terrified them. Because the one they knew so well had become the one they could not easily control. So they pushed back. Their skepticism hardened into offense. And Jesus did not perform for them. He did not argue His own credibility. He simply told them what they already felt: a prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house.

Two stories. Two places of worship. Two moments of rejection. Two messengers who carried the same Word. And two truths that reach across the centuries to stand before each of us.

When God speaks, do we listen — or do we reach for our own certainty? When Christ comes to us in familiar form, in ordinary places, through ordinary means, do we honor Him — or do we take offense because He does not arrive the way we expected?

Jeremiah was spared because the elders remembered Micah. They remembered that God had spoken before, and that God always speaks through those He sends, not those we approve. Jesus was limited in Nazareth, not because His power was insufficient, but because their hearts were closed. Faith opens the door. Unbelief locks it.

The same choice stands before us today. Before this Word, in this moment, where do we stand? Are we like the officials who listened, the elders who remembered, the few who protected the prophet's voice? Or are we like the crowd in the temple who wanted to silence God, or the neighbors in Nazareth who refused to be astonished?

The Lord does not force His way into our lives. He stands and speaks. Then He gives us space — the holy space of a free heart — to answer. The question is whether we will use that space to receive Him or to reject Him.

His Word endures. Whether we listen or not, whether we honor Him or not, He speaks still. And in the stillness of our hearts, if we are willing to listen, we may hear what Jeremiah spoke and what Jesus proclaimed: the Lord desires mercy, not sacrifice. He desires a heart that listens, a soul that trusts, a life that follows — even when the world does not understand.

---

## PART 6 — LIFE APPLICATION

1. Examine your own readiness to hear God's word. Are you like the people of Jerusalem, so wrapped in religious routine that God's real challenge becomes a threat? Make space in your daily life for Scripture that unsettles and renews you.

2. Do not dismiss the familiar as ordinary. The people of Nazareth knew Jesus personally and refused to believe. Look at your own family, parish, and community with fresh eyes — Christ may be working among those you take for granted.

3. When others are criticized for speaking the truth, stand with courage like Ahikam son of Shaphan. Protect the voice of truth in your community, defend the vulnerable, and remember that faithfulness to God sometimes means standing against the crowd.

4. Guard your heart against the offense of familiarity. Repeated exposure to the sacraments, the Mass, the Scriptures can quietly numb spiritual sight. Ask the Lord to rekindle wonder in your faith — to make you astonished again by the One who walks beside you every day.

5. Trust that God's Word will accomplish its purpose, regardless of human resistance. Where you feel rejected, silenced, or dismissed — God's truth remains firm. Rest in His faithfulness, not in the approval of others.

---

## PART 7 — PRAYER

Lord God, You who spoke through Jeremiah in the temple courts and through Jesus in the synagogue of Nazareth, we come before You with humble and open hearts. We confess that we, too, are quick to close our ears when Your Word disturbs our comfort — and that we, too, can take offense at the familiar face of Christ in those around us. Forgive us for our unbelief, for our stubbornness, for the times we prefer our own understanding over Your truth. Like the elders who remembered Micah, help us remember all that You have done and all that You have spoken. Make us a people who listen, who trust, and who honor the messengers You send — even when their words cost us something. Open our hearts to the fullness of Christ's presence, in the Scriptures, in the Sacraments, and in every neighbor You place along our path. We ask this through Christ our Lord, who speaks the truth and loves us without measure. Amen.

---
